items.title: Fed minutes October 2026: Officials expect more rate hikes, worry about AI
items.excerpt: Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday. Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk." More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December. The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."

items.title: The US Fed's next move could be bigger as inflation refuses to retreat, minutes show - The Economic Times
items.excerpt: Washington: Federal Reserve officials saw a growing risk last month that they might need to intensify ... "Almost all" policymakers agreed that further rate hikes would be needed if the economy evolved as they expected, the minutes said, while a few said inflation could prove more persistent and require "a shift to a more restrictive policy stance" than currently expected. "A couple" of them went further and argued that the Fed might have to resort to a half-percentage-point increase "if incoming inflation data were unfavorable," a benchmark met in recent releases that showed prices rising faster than anticipated. Among those who supported keeping the policy rate steady in the 3.75%-4.00% range in October, "a few ... indicated that they viewed the decision as a close call," and joined a larger group in urging that the Fed be clear that "the decision to maintain the target range did not reflect a weakening" of the commitment to hit the US central bank's 2% inflation target. At the end of the two-day session, only Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of lifting the policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point. But the debate highlighted a growing sense at the Fed that inflation will not ease enough on its own for the target to be reached quickly enough.

items.title: Core inflation is 0.5 point lower by CPI than by PCE, and Fed minutes call it unusual | FinanceInTime
items.excerpt: ## Total inflation barely differs, core inflation does The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7% in the 12 months to September, after 3.4% in the 12 months to August. The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said the PCE price index, its measure of prices for personal consumption expenditures, rose 3.6% from a year earlier in September, after 3.4% in August. Excluding food and energy, the picture splits. Core CPI rose 2.6% over the year to September, following 2.4% in August. Core PCE rose 3.1% in September, after 3.0% in August. Subtracting, the core CPI ran 0.5 percentage point below core PCE in September and 0.6 point below in August (computed from the four published rates). Total CPI was 0.1 point above total PCE in September and equal to it in August (computed). The Fed sets its 2% goal in PCE terms: the Committee judges that inflation at 2% "as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures" fits its mandate over the longer run. So the measure with the higher core reading is the one the Committee targets. ## What the monthly figures show The gap is not a story of one month. In September the CPI rose 0.6% on the month, seasonally adjusted, and the PCE price index rose 0.5%. Both core measures rose 0.3% in September. In August, core CPI rose 0.3% while core PCE rose 0.2%, the BEA said. Energy was the main driver of the headline. The BLS said gasoline rose 9.1% in September and accounted for over half of the monthly increase in the all-items index, and the energy index rose 5.2% on the month and 20.4% over the 12 months to September. Energy carries a different weight in each index, and the releases do not state the weights, so the data here do not show how much of the headline similarity comes from energy. ... The October CPI report shows the CPI rose 0.4% on the month after 0.6% in September, with core prices up 0.3% for a third month. The BLS said it did not collect survey data for October 2025 because of a lapse in appropriations, so it cannot publish 12-month changes for October 2026 for indexes where October 2025 data are unavailable. The annual CPI comparison with PCE therefore stops at September until November data arrive; the BEA's October PCE release is due on November 25, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. EST, according to its September release. ## What Fed officials said about the discrepancy The minutes of the Fed's October 27-28 meeting, released on November 18, show the staff estimated PCE inflation of 3.6% in September and core PCE of 3.1%, and attributed higher inflation largely to earlier tariff increases, higher energy prices and upward pressure on goods prices tied to the AI buildout. Some participants raised the gap directly. A few cautioned that market-based inflation expectations, derived from the pricing of securities indexed to the CPI, "might be difficult to interpret" given "an unusual discrepancy between CPI and PCE inflation rates." The minutes do not say what causes the discrepancy. Participants also pointed to elevated inflation in market-based core nonhousing services and to measures of underlying inflation that remained above 2%. Almost all judged that further action to raise the target range would likely be appropriate, and a couple said an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the next meeting if inflation data were unfavorable. That meeting is on December 8-9.

items.title: Republicans lose hope in Reconciliation 3.0
items.excerpt: The Senate GOP's last-ditch effort to pass a defense-heavy, $350 billion reconciliation package is dead on arrival without accompanying spending cuts, House Republicans tell Axios. Why it matters: House Republicans have just 16 days left in session before Democrats take control in January. Many don't want to spend their final days in power adding to the national debt. - "My concern is we squander these very few days we have left on something that won't get out of the House," outgoing House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas) told Axios of the Senate's emerging plan. - Republicans have already passed two party-line reconciliation bills this Congress: The "one big, beautiful bill" in the summer of 2025, and nearly $70 billion for immigration enforcement in the summer of 2026. Zoom in: Finding spending offsets could reopen some of the most contentious fights from the GOP's first reconciliation package. - Arrington told Axios that Senate Republicans worry that finding cost savings in health care spending could open the door to amendment votes that undo Medicaid cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. - But Arrington, who didn't run for reelection in 2026, told Axios he doesn't believe the Senate's proposal has the votes to pass the House without offsets. State of play: Arrington said he raised his concerns with Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), and argued Republicans shouldn't let the risks deter them from pursuing additional spending cuts. - "Some Republican members of the Senate might go rogue and might decide to, I don't know, repeal some of the reforms that we put in the 'big, beautiful bill.' Maybe they do it out of spite for President Trump," he said. - "The midterms have passed us. We lost, but we still have this window to do what we think is right," he said. Between the lines: Senate Republicans haven't committed to moving forward with another reconciliation package. - Leaving a Wednesday night meeting on reconciliation, Sen. Johnson told reporters the Senate "probably" won't move forward this week, but a reconciliation bill isn't "off the table." - Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters he wants to explore working with Democrats on the funding, but that reconciliation remains an "option" Wednesday night. What they're saying: "It needs to have offsets," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.), a member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, told Axios. - Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.), another HFC member, also expressed skepticism about the proposal and its chances of passage. "It's not that I don't want to fund the Department of Defense, but it's always, 'Hey, are we just going to add this to the debt, add this to the deficit,'" he told Axios. The intrigue: Even if the two chambers can strike a deal, House GOP leaders are struggling to get their own members to show up for votes. - GOP leaders were forced to pull a procedural rule vote Wednesday after 14 Republicans failed to show up, leaving leadership without the votes needed to move forward. - Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios his colleagues need to return to Washington: "I mean, they're getting paid until Jan. 3." What's next: The House departs Thursday for Thanksgiving recess.

items.excerpt: Skydance names ‌film chiefs ​for Paramount, Warner Bros labels Skydance named Don Granger and Kira Goldberg presidents of the Motion Picture Group at Paramount Pictures, while promoting Jesse Ehrman to president of the Motion Picture Group at Warner Bros Pictures, outlining the leadership structure for its combined film business. The changes come as Skydance seeks to build a company capable of delivering 30 films a year, with Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros Pictures retaining separate identities and distinct creative mandates, according to an internal memo to staff on Tuesday from Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. ... 'GTA VI' to supercharge Sony — just not in Japan The global launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" on Thursday is expected to provide a major boost to PlayStation maker Sony -- albeit not in its home market of ‌Japan, where the franchise is a niche pursuit. The long-awaited open-world crime action game from Take-Two Interactive's Rockstar Games is rolling out across the world and has been met with rave reviews and fans taking time off work to play. Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Cher to headline UK's Glastonbury in 2027 Harry Styles, Sam Fender, Billie Eilish and Cher will headline Britain's Glastonbury next year, the organisers said on their website on Wednesday, as the sold-out festival returns after taking a year off in 2026. British singer Harry Styles, who recently completed a 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden in New York, will play the festival for the first time, while Cher will take the legends slot at the age of 81. ... Spain's High Court opens investigation into women's allegations against Julio Iglesias A Spanish High Court judge has opened a criminal investigation into singer Julio Iglesias after a complaint filed by two former employees alleging sexual offences, assault and degrading treatment, court records showed. The complaint was filed by ⁠rights group Women's Link Worldwide on behalf of two women who said they worked in Iglesias' Caribbean residences for 10 months in 2021, following an investigation by US broadcaster Univision and Spanish outlet elDiario.es. Ariana Grande and Ben Stiller feud in 'Focker In-Law' with flipped roles A battle of wits pits singer and actor Ariana Grande against Hollywood star and filmmaker Ben Stiller in "Focker In-Law". The fourth installment in the "Fockers" comedy film franchise comes 26 years after Stiller and Robert De Niro introduced audiences ⁠to ​quarrelling male nurse Greg Focker and retired CIA operative Jack Byrnes in "Meet the Parents".

The film also features Mysskin in a lead role. ... ## Ramayana Box Office Collection Day 14 Ramayana has surpassed Aditya Dhar's Dhurandhar at the Indian box office within just two weeks of its release. According to Sacnilk, the film earned Rs. 23.20 crore net in India on Day 14, taking its total domestic net collection to Rs. 844.40 crore. Its India gross collection has now reached Rs. 1,009.05 crore. With this, Ramayana has moved ahead of Dhurandhar, which had collected Rs. 840.20 crore net in India after its release in December last year. The achievement comes just 14 days into Ramayana's theatrical run. However, the film's overseas performance appears to be slowing down. It added Rs. 8 crore gross from international markets on Day 14, taking its overseas gross collection to Rs. 510 crore. Meanwhile, its worldwide gross collection has reached Rs. 1,519.05 crore. Speaking to TIME magazine as part of its TIME100 Next India feature, Alia Bhatt addressed the online discussions about her marriage to Ranbir Kapoor and the claims that she is in an ‘unequal marriage’. The actress called such assumptions offensive, saying people were reducing her to someone who would silently suffer in an imaginary situation. Alia also suggested that the speculation could stem from the fact that her relationship does not follow conventional ideas of marriage. Explaining what makes her bond with Ranbir special, she said, "The bedrock of any relationship is when you feel seen without putting any effort, and feel heard without saying anything—that’s Ranbir for me, and that’s our reality." ...
